ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A point mass is thrown from the ground with initial velocity $\vec{v}_{0}$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. Assume air friction is negligible unless stated otherwise. When friction is considered, the equation of motion is given by $\frac{d \vec{v}}{d t}=\vec{g}-\beta \vec{v}$, where $\beta$ is a constant.

1. (a) What value of $\theta$ maximizes the range?
2. (b) What value of $\theta$ maximizes the surface area under the trajectory curve?
3. (c) If the point mass is thrown from an apartment of height $h$, what value of $\theta$ maximizes the range?
4. (d) Supposing that $\beta \ll \frac{g}{v_{0}}$, find the duration of the motion $T$.

Assume air friction is negligible unless stated otherwise. ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: No image evidence is needed; the problem is text-only. For parts (a) and (b), neglect air resistance and use the standard projectile equations for launch from the ground: x(t)=v0 cosθ · t and y(t)=v0 sinθ · t − (1/2)gt². Eliminating t gives y(x)=x tanθ − g x²/(2v0² cos²θ). (a) At landing on the ground, y=0 with x=R>0. Thus R(θ)=v0² sin(2θ)/g. Maximizing R requires sin(2θ)=1, so 2θ=π/2 and θ=π/4. (b) The area under the trajectory is A(θ)=∫ from 0 to R of y(x) dx. Using y(x)=x tanθ − g x²/(2v0² cos²θ) and R=2v0² sinθ cosθ/g, this simplifies to A(θ)=(2v0⁴/(3g²)) sin³θ cosθ. Therefore maximize f(θ)=sin³θ cosθ. Its derivative is f'(θ)=3sin²θ cos²θ − sin⁴θ=sin²θ(3cos²θ−sin²θ). For a nonzero trajectory, 3cos²θ=sin²θ, so tan²θ=3 and θ=π/3. (c) For launch from height h, use y(x)=h+x tanθ − g x²/(2v0² cos²θ). Equivalently, the flight time to the ground satisfies h+v0 sinθ · t − (1/2)gt²=0, so t=[v0 sinθ + sqrt(v0² sin²θ+2gh)]/g. The range is R(θ)=(v0 cosθ/g)[v0 sinθ + sqrt(v0² sin²θ+2gh)]. Differentiating this range with respect to θ and setting the derivative to zero gives sinθ = v0/[√2 sqrt(v0²+gh)]. Hence θ=arcsin(v0/[√2 sqrt(v0²+gh)]). (d) For the drag case, take the vertical component with upward y positive: dv_y/dt = −g − βv_y. Since β << g/v0, the intended approximate treatment estimates the leading drag correction by using the characteristic initial upward vertical speed v0 sinθ in the small drag term, rather than solving the full time-dependent drag problem. With this heuristic leading-denominator approximation, the vertical motion is treated as having effective downward acceleration g+βv0 sinθ. Then setting the vertical displacement back to zero gives 0=v0 sinθ · T − (1/2)(g+βv0 sinθ)T². The nonzero flight time is therefore T=2v0 sinθ/(g+βv0 sinθ) = [2v0 sinθ/g]/[1+βv0 sinθ/g].
